title: CQRS

validation.research: Six primary sources: Greg Young’s CQRS Documents (printed pages 17–23), Martin Fowler’s CQRS and Command Query Separation entries, Microsoft’s CQRS documentation, SQLite Transactions, and Python sqlite3 documentation. Canonical CQRS and long-form aliases are preserved. The article distinguishes method-level CQS from model-level segregation, shared-store from separate-store choices, Event Sourcing from CQRS, fresh shared-store statements from retained old DTOs, and observation versions from checked command preconditions.

runnable_example.verification: Exact demo output; query projection bypasses SeatPool without mutating store; frozen old DTO and frozen value-based command model; normal command completion returns None after commit; fresh read sees version 1 while kept DTO stays at version 0; sold-out rejection leaves count/version unchanged; unrelated show isolation; read-only URI write rejection; reopened read consistency; exact 1/1000-seat and 64/65-character boundaries; invalid quantity/ID and missing-show rejection without mutation; concurrent writers cannot overbook; forced update-error rollback of count and version; abrupt pre-commit process exit recovery; busy-BEGIN and failed-COMMIT rollback with later successful retry; parameterized title data; repeated successful commands intentionally are not deduplicated. No asynchronous projection, event log, authentication, or booking lifecycle is inferred.

example_limits: Original standard-library Python 3.11+ SQLite example of shared-storage model separation. SeatPool validates 1–1000 physical seats; the query builds a separate frozen Availability DTO directly from SQL. BEGIN IMMEDIATE serializes writers before reading current capacity; a dedicated idle write connection owns one command transaction. Count/version commit or roll back together. Read-only URI prevents accidental writes but supplies no full authentication/process security boundary. Returned DTOs remain immutable snapshots, fresh autocommit queries see committed state, and stored versions are observations rather than expected-version checks. Normal public command completion returns None after commit. No individual booking records, payment, authentication, event log, asynchronous read store, projection worker, cancellation lifecycle, retry deduplication, or network effects. Concurrent writers, forced statement and commit failures, busy BEGIN, abrupt pre-commit process exit, reopened connections, and invalid boundaries are verified; no production power-loss or distributed recovery claim.
